title.en: Types of farming and cropping seasons

text.en: A tribal farmer in Assam clears forest for Jhum cultivation, while a hill farmer cuts terraces. India shows many ways of farming.

Agriculture is producing food, fodder and fibre by growing crops and raising livestock.
Agriculture is determined by physical (relief, climate, soil), institutional (land holdings, tenure), infrastructural (irrigation, power, credit) and technological factors.
Subsistence farming uses family labour and traditional methods; most produce is consumed by the family.
Shifting agriculture (slash and burn) is called Jhum in Assam, Poonam in Kerala and Podu in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Intensive farming uses heavy pesticides and fertilizers to maximise yield from available land.
Dry farming is practised in arid areas without irrigation, with drought-resistant crops and usually one crop a year.
Mixed farming combines crops with livestock, poultry, fisheries and bee keeping.
Terrace farming is used on hill slopes where flat land is scarce and also checks soil erosion.
Cropping seasons: Kharif (June to September), Rabi (October to March) and Zaid (April to June).

problem.en: Classify rice, wheat and watermelon by cropping season and justify.

text.en: Rice is mostly a Kharif crop, sown with the monsoon in June and harvested in autumn.
Wheat is a Rabi crop sown in October and harvested by March.
Vegetables and fruits like watermelon are Zaid crops grown in summer.

prompt.en: Why is shifting cultivation considered harmful?

requiredIdeas.en: Fertility drops after two or three years
Farmers move on, causing deforestation and erosion

points.en: Subsistence, shifting, intensive, dry, mixed, terrace farming.
Jhum = Assam, Podu = Andhra and Odisha.
